25-1311.facts:
Apple's App Store is the only way to download apps onto iPhones in the United States. Apple takes a 15-30% commission on digital goods purchased through the App Store, and its anti-steering provisions blocked developers from directing users to cheaper purchasing options outside the App Store.

In 2020, Epic Games, one of the largest mobile game developers and distributor of its own competing app marketplace, sued Apple under federal antitrust law and California's Unfair Competition Law (UCL). The district court rejected the federal claims but agreed that the anti-steering rules violated the UCL by preventing consumers from learning about lower-priced alternatives. It issued a 75-word [permanent injunction](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.364265/gov.uscourts.cand.364265.813.0_3.pdf) barring Apple from prohibiting developers from including buttons, external links, or other calls to action directing users to alternative purchasing mechanisms. The injunction said nothing about commissions. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court declined review in January 2024.

That same day, Apple announced that it would comply by allowing developers to add links. However, Apple charged up to a 27% commission on purchases made through external links, and it limited how the links looked and where they appeared.

Epic asked the district court to hold Apple in civil contempt, arguing that the commission and restrictions defeated the injunction's purpose even though the text never addressed commissions. In April 2025, the court agreed. It found that two of Apple's link-design rules were "explicitly at odds" with the injunction's text, and that the commission and the remaining restrictions violated the injunction's spirit by foreclosing alternatives to Apple's payment system. Relying in part on Apple's internal documents, it found that Apple chose the commission to make linking economically unviable for developers and designed the restrictions to discourage customers from using links, picking the most anticompetitive option it considered, and that Apple had willfully violated the injunction. [The Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2025/12/11/25-2935.pdf), holding that a party can be held in contempt for violating an injunction's spirit, not only its words. It also reasoned that the 27% commission had a "prohibitive effect" that the injunction's bar on "prohibiting" links forbade.
25-1311.background:
Courts can hold a party in civil contempt for disobeying a court order, which can carry fines or other sanctions to force compliance. The [history](https://www.fjc.gov/history/work-courts/contempt-power-federal-courts) of the courts' contempt power is complex, but the Supreme Court has consistently stated that all courts possess contempt power [inherently](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artIII-S1-4-3/ALDE_00013522/).

Because violating an injunction can lead to contempt, [Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65(d)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_65) requires every injunction to "state its terms specifically" and "describe in reasonable detail" the conduct it restrains or requires. In [*Taggart v. Lorenzen*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/587/18-489/) (2019), a case about bankruptcy orders, the Supreme Court explained that civil contempt traditionally "should not be resorted to where there is [a] fair ground of doubt as to the wrongfulness of the defendant's conduct." The standard is generally objective: a party's sincere belief that it was complying won't protect it if that belief was unreasonable.

25-5343.background:
In 1984, Congress created the U.S. Sentencing Commission—an independent agency in the judicial branch—to write rules making federal sentences more uniform. Since 1987, the Commission has published the Federal Sentencing Guidelines, along with official commentary that explains and interprets them. Judges must begin every federal sentencing by correctly calculating the range the Guidelines recommend. In [*Stinson v. United States*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/508/36/) (1993), the Supreme Court held that the commentary is a mandatory part of that calculation unless it violates the Constitution or a federal law or is plainly wrong or inconsistent with the Guideline it interprets. In doing so, the Supreme Court borrowed the rule it had set for federal agencies in [*Bowles v. Seminole Rock & Sand Co.*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/325/410/) (1945): an agency's interpretation of its own regulation controls "unless it is plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation."

In [*United States v. Booker*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/543/220/) (2005), the Supreme Court made the Guidelines advisory, so while judges must still begin sentencing by calculating the recommended range, they may choose sentences outside that range.

In [*Kisor v. Wilkie*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/588/18-15/) (2019), the Supreme Court declined to abandon the standard in *Seminole Rock* but reinforced its limits, allowing deference only when (1) a regulation is genuinely ambiguous, (2) the agency's reading is reasonable, and (3) the reading reflects the agency's official, expert, and considered judgment. Federal appeals courts have disagreed about whether those limits also apply to the commentary.
25-5343.facts:
Kendrick Beaird pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm as a convicted felon. The district court applied a sentencing enhancement because Beaird's gun could accept a "large capacity magazine." The Guidelines do not define that term, but the commentary says it covers any magazine holding more than 15 rounds, and Beaird's held 17. Beaird objected to the court's reliance on the commentary's definition. The district court sentenced him to 72 months in prison, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that *Stinson* was unaffected by *Kisor*.

At the Supreme Court, Beaird argues that the commentary deserves no deference. The government argues that, after *Kisor*, courts should defer only after finding genuine ambiguity in the Guidelines. The Supreme Court appointed an outside lawyer to defend the Fifth Circuit's view that the commentary controls unless it is inconsistent with the Guidelines or plainly wrong.

25-735.background:
Federal district courts have "original jurisdiction of all civil actions arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States." [28 U.S.C. § 1331](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/1331). Therefore, by default, they can review constitutional challenges to statutes unless some other statute withdraws that jurisdiction expressly or by implication.

Veterans with service-connected disabilities can apply for monthly benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). Since the 1930s, federal law—in a section known as the "no-review clause"—has barred federal courts from reviewing the VA's benefits decisions. The version in effect in 1974 provided that:

> "[T]he decisions of the Administrator on any question of law or fact under any law administered by the Veterans' Administration providing benefits for veterans . . . shall be final and conclusive and no other official or any court of the United States shall have power or jurisdiction to review any such decision[.]"

In [*Johnson v. Robison*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/415/361/) (1974), the Supreme Court held this earlier version of that clause did not stop federal courts from reviewing the constitutionality of veterans' benefits legislation, but instead only restricted judicial review of individual administrative decisions made by the VA. The Court reasoned that the clause covered decisions made "under" a law the VA administered, and a challenge to the law's constitutionality arises under the Constitution instead.

In 1988, Congress passed the [VJRA](https://www.congress.gov/100/statute/STATUTE-102/STATUTE-102-Pg4105.pdf), which—among other things—created a new path for appealing benefits decisions: from the Board of Veterans' Appeals (BVA) to a new Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC), and then to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which it gave exclusive authority over challenges to the validity of veterans' benefits statutes in appeals from the CAVC. It also rewrote the language of the "no-review clause," now at [38 U.S.C. § 511(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/511), to read as follows:

> "The Secretary shall decide all questions of law and fact necessary to a decision by the Secretary under a law that affects the provision of benefits by the Secretary to veterans . . . . Subject to [certain exceptions, including review through the VJRA's appeals scheme], the decision of the Secretary as to any such question shall be final and conclusive and may not be reviewed by any other official or by any court[.]"

25-735.facts:
Floyd Johnson, a U.S. Army veteran, began receiving disability benefits for service-related post-traumatic stress disorder while serving a 40-year prison sentence in Florida. While the VA approved an 80 percent disability rating and associated benefits, it later reduced his benefits to the level of a 10 percent disability rating. It cited a benefits cap at [38 U.S.C. § 5313](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/5313), which limits disability compensation for veterans incarcerated for more than 60 days following a felony conviction.

Johnson sued Congress, arguing that the law violates the Constitution's [bill of attainder clause](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S9-C3-2/ALDE_00013187/) (which prohibits laws that punish a specific group without a trial), as well as the [Fifth Amendment](https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-5/)'s guarantee of equal protection. He did not challenge how the VA handled his own claim. The district court assumed it had jurisdiction to hear the case but dismissed it on the merits. On appeal, the Eleventh Circuit held that Congress couldn't be sued due to sovereign immunity, but it did not grant Johnson's request to substitute the VA as a defendant. Instead, it vacated the judgment and ordered the case dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, ruling that the VJRA strips district courts of jurisdiction to hear constitutional challenges to veterans' benefits legislation.

25-170.background:
**The Clean Air Act**

The [Clean Air Act of 1970](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/clean_air_act_%28caa%29) (CAA) allowed the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to set air quality standards for air pollutants. In 2009, following [*Massachusetts v. EPA*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/549/497/) (2007)—where the Supreme Court held that greenhouse gases are "air pollutants" under the CAA—the EPA signed the [Endangerment Finding](https://www.epa.gov/climate-change/endangerment-and-cause-or-contribute-findings-greenhouse-gases-under-section-202a), which found that greenhouse gas emissions from new motor vehicles endangered public health and welfare. The EPA later signed final rules with similar findings for emissions from [power plants](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2015/10/23/2015-22837/standards-of-performance-for-greenhouse-gas-emissions-from-new-modified-and-reconstructed-stationary) (2015) and [aircraft](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2016/08/15/2016-18399/finding-that-greenhouse-gas-emissions-from-aircraft-cause-or-contribute-to-air-pollution-that-may) (2016).

In February 2026, the EPA [rescinded](https://www.epa.gov/regulations-emissions-vehicles-and-engines/final-rule-rescission-greenhouse-gas-endangerment) the 2009 finding and repealed all federal vehicle greenhouse-gas standards, concluding that the CAA does not authorize it to regulate those emissions to address global climate change. In September 2026, the EPA [repealed](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/17/2026-19071/partial-repeal-of-the-carbon-pollution-standards-for-fossil-fuel-fired-electric-generating-units) most power-plant greenhouse-gas standards and [proposed rescinding](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/17/2026-19072/rescission-of-the-greenhouse-gas-findings-for-fossil-fuel-fired-power-plants-and-repeal-of) the 2015 findings on the same rationale; that proposal is not yet final.

**Preemption**

The supremacy clause—the second sentence in [Article VI of the Constitution](https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/article-6/)—provides that the Constitution, and laws and treaties made pursuant to it, is the supreme law of the land. If there is a conflict between federal and state law, the federal law controls and the state law is invalidated. There are generally two kinds of preemption: (1) where a federal law expressly preempts state or local law; and (2) where preemption is implied by clear congressional intent to preempt. The three most common types of implied preemption are (a) conflict preemption, where federal and state laws are mutually exclusive; (b) obstacle preemption, where the state or local law interferes with achieving a federal objective; and (c) field preemption, where Congress has evidenced a clear intent to have federal law wholly occupy that area of law.

There is another unusual form of implied preemption: foreign affairs preemption. For example, in [*Zschernig v. Miller*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/389/429/) (1968), the Supreme Court struck down an Oregon inheritance law for intruding on foreign affairs without relying on any conflicting treaty or statute (["dormant" foreign affairs preemption](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10808)). In [*American Insurance Association v. Garamendi*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/539/396/) (2003), the Supreme Court invalidated California's Holocaust Victim Insurance Relief Act, which required insurers doing business in California to disclose information about European policies in effect from 1920 to 1945, because it conflicted with executive agreements the President had negotiated on Holocaust-era insurance claims.

Preemption can also occur through federal common law. Federal common law is law made by federal courts, rather than Congress, in narrow areas involving uniquely federal interests. This includes interstate pollution: In [*Illinois v. Milwaukee*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/406/91/) (1972), the Supreme Court recognized a federal common-law nuisance claim for interstate water pollution. In [*American Electric Power Co. v. Connecticut*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/564/410/) (2011) (*AEP*), it held that the CAA displaced federal common-law claims over greenhouse-gas emissions, because Congress delegated to the EPA the decisions whether and how to regulate them. *AEP* left open whether the CAA also preempts state-law claims, and lower courts have split on that question.

**Jurisdiction**

Congress allows the Supreme Court to review state-court decisions under [28 U.S.C. § 1257(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/1257#a), which requires that the decision from the state's highest court be a "final judgment" resolving a federal issue—[meaning](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/final_judgment) a last decision from a court that resolves all issues in the dispute and settles the parties' rights with respect to those issues, leaving only decisions on how to enforce the judgment, whether to award costs, and whether to file an appeal. In [*Cox Broadcasting Corp. v. Cohn*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/420/469/) (1975), the Supreme Court recognized four exceptions allowing review even when further proceedings remain in state court: (1) where the federal issue is conclusive of the case outcome or the outcome of further proceedings is preordained; (2) where the state court's decision on the federal issue will survive and require decision regardless of how remaining state proceedings turn out; (3) where later federal review of the federal issue will be unavailable; and (4) where the federal issue was finally decided, reversal would end the litigation, and refusing immediate review might seriously erode federal policy.

[Article III of the Constitution](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artIII-S2-C1-6-1/ALDE_00012992/) gives federal courts power to decide only actual "cases" or "controversies." The concept of "standing" is how the courts apply this requirement: in general, it requires a party to establish (1) a concrete and particularized injury; (2) that is traceable to the allegedly unlawful actions of the opposing party; and (3) that is redressable by a favorable judicial decision. While state courts are not bound by Article III, a party asking for the Supreme Court to review a state-court decision must itself have Article III standing.
25-170.facts:
Suncor Energy, Inc. (Suncor) is one of Canada's largest energy companies, and several of its U.S.-based subsidiaries operate Colorado's only oil refinery. Exxon Mobil Corporation (Exxon) is the largest U.S.-based oil company.

In 2018, the city and county of Boulder filed a lawsuit in state court against Exxon and some of Suncor's U.S.-based subsidiaries, seeking compensation for costs they incurred protecting their property and residents from the alleged effects of climate change. Boulder brought several claims under Colorado state law, including public nuisance, private nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, and civil conspiracy. Boulder claims that the companies knowingly contributed to climate change while misleading the public about the dangers of their products. Boulder seeks to recover millions of dollars spent protecting property and residents from the effects of climate change such as wildfires, flooding, and drought. Boulder does not seek to enjoin any oil and gas operations or sales, and it does not seek to enforce emissions controls of any kind.

The energy companies tried and failed to transfer ("remove") the case to federal court. The county trial court then denied the companies' request to dismiss Boulder's state common-law claims on federal preemption grounds. The companies then petitioned the Colorado Supreme Court under [Colorado Appellate Rule 21](https://www.courtrules.net/colorado/colorado-appellate-procedure/rule-21), which governs that court's original proceedings for extraordinary relief, asking the court to dismiss the case on federal preemption grounds. The Colorado Supreme Court concluded that federal law did not preempt Boulder's claims and allowed the case to continue.

The energy companies petitioned the Supreme Court to hear the case. Shortly before oral argument, Justice Alito recused himself after scrutiny of his holdings in other oil and gas companies facing similar suits. A 4-4 tie would leave in place the Colorado Supreme Court's decision without setting nationwide precedent, allowing Boulder's claims to proceed. This case is one of dozens of similar state-law climate tort suits that state and local governments have filed against energy companies across the country.

25-498.background:
The [Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/erisa) (ERISA) is a federal statute that, among other things, delineates minimum standards for the administration of private industry's pension plans. ERISA establishes a "duty of prudence," which requires plan fiduciaries to act "with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence" that a prudent person "acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a like character and with like aims." [29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1104).

The Supreme Court has addressed how the duty of prudence applies when courts decide whether a complaint states an ERISA claim. In [*Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/573/409/) (2014), it explained that the prudence inquiry "will necessarily be context specific." In [*Hughes v. Northwestern University*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/595/19-1401/) (2022), it rejected a lower court's rule that participants' ability to choose their own investments excused imprudent options in a plan, calling that "categorical rule" "inconsistent with the context-specific inquiry that ERISA requires," while also cautioning that courts "must give due regard to the range of reasonable judgments a fiduciary may make."

Many—but not all—federal appellate courts have adopted a "meaningful benchmark" standard for claims based on a fund's underperformance, although courts differ on the contours of that standard and whether a benchmark is always strictly mandatory. That standard requires plaintiffs to point to an appropriate comparator investment that is sufficiently similar to the challenged investment—in terms of aims, risks, investment strategy, and potential rewards—to serve as a legitimate basis for inferring fiduciary imprudence from alleged underperformance of the challenged investment. The standard generally serves as a threshold pleading requirement: before a plaintiff can proceed to discovery on a claim of imprudent fund selection, they must identify an alternative investment that provides a sound basis for comparison to the challenged investment.
25-498.facts:
Winston Anderson, an Intel employee from 2000 to 2015, participated in two Intel retirement plans: the Intel 401(k) Savings Plan and the Intel Retirement Contribution Plan. After the 2008 financial crisis, Intel started allocating some of its investment funds to hedge funds and private equity, in addition to traditional assets like stocks and bonds. Intel disclosed at the time that the strategy was intended to reduce the risk of large losses, and that the funds "would not compare favorably with equity-heavy funds during bull markets." Anderson alleges that the funds then lagged equity-heavy funds during the market upswings that followed.

In 2019, Anderson sued on behalf of a group of retirement plan participants. He alleges, among other claims, that Intel's strategy deviated from industry standards and led to persistently poor returns due to excessive risk and high fees, and therefore breached ERISA's duty of prudence.

The district court dismissed the case, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal. It held that when a plaintiff relies on underperformance or excessive fees to infer imprudence rather than directly alleging improper process, the complaint must identify a "meaningful benchmark" against which to compare the fund's performance; only then can a court infer that the fiduciary's process was imprudent. It held that Anderson had failed to state a claim because his comparators pursued different investment objectives—specifically, generating higher returns rather than risk mitigation—and therefore were not meaningfully similar to Intel's funds.
